title: CR-017 Pigment Beneath the Plaster
description: Original Tang-informed secular mineral-pigment mural study as the principal image: three restrained adult attendants in a planar procession with limited painted timber architectural motifs on prepared plaster. Uses new_generation, EraPack tang, ArtMethod mineral_pigment_mural, artifact form wall_surface, and state newly_created. The composition includes one small deliberate unfinished workshop margin revealing prepared ground and a narrow plaster strip without artificial aging. No TransformationPack, reference images, Dunhuang site pack, or APCC.

semantic_spec.request: Create an original Tang-informed secular mineral-pigment wall painting as the principal image filling a 4:5 field. The mural itself occupies nearly the entire frame as a continuous wall-bound painting on prepared plaster—not a photograph of a museum installation, not a living corridor scene, not a framed canvas, not a fashion portrait, and not a sacred cave-temple reconstruction. Depict three restrained adult attendants in a quiet planar procession among limited painted architectural motifs (suggested timber-post and lintel geometry as painted wall decoration, not deep photographic perspective). Figures remain subordinate to the wall-painting program: planar contours, matte mineral color fields, and hierarchical wall composition rather than photographic depth or garment spectacle. Material construction order is architectural wall support, then earthen plaster, then prepared painting ground, then line drawing and mineral-pigment layers. The painting is freshly completed and newly created: intact ground and pigment, clean workshop-fresh finish, no centuries of weathering, no soot, no salt damage, no random flaking, no excavated losses, and no conservation patches. Where ArtMethod fragments mention localized loss, cracks, or aging, treat those as generic method vocabulary for other states—not instructions for this image—and obey artifact state newly_created instead. Demonstrate material construction without damage by keeping the completed painted program dominant while reserving one small deliberate unfinished lower-left margin where unpainted prepared ground and a narrow strip of earthen plaster remain visible as a workshop edge, not as archaeological damage. Prefer matte mineral pigment opacity and fine granular character, brush-defined contours integrated with plaster grain, and limited organic-wash suggestion only where subordinate to mineral fields. Do not invent sacred deities, mudras, halo programs, calligraphy, seals, artist attribution, logos, or fake inscriptions.
